To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the majority of HCV-specific effector CD8+T cells undergo massive apoptosis in the peripheral blood during the acute stage of HCV infection and in the infected liver during the chronic stage of HCV.
the majority of HCV-specific effector CD8+T cells in the blood of patients during acute HCV infections and in the liver of patients with chronic HCV infections are undergoing apoptosis.
HCV-specific CD 8+ T cells undergo massive apoptosis in the liver during chronic infection, and in the blood during both acute and chronic infection.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of apoptosis in the regulation of T-cell responses during HCV infection.
the immune response to hepatitis C virus ( HCV ) infection, which is characterized by the inability of the majority of infected patients to clear the virus.
the mechanisms of T-cell dysfunction and the role of T-cell apoptosis in HCV infection.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the HCV-specific T-cell response during acute infection is impaired by apoptosis of activated CD8+ T lymphocytes.
the majority of HCV-specific effector T cells undergo apoptosis during both the acute and chronic phases of infection, which leads to a contraction of the HCV specific CD8 T-cell population.
the HCV-specific T-cell response is not able to control HCV infection and that this is because of the inability of HCV-specific T cells to survive and function.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
HCV-specific CD4 and CD8 T cell responses are activated during the acute phase, but the majority of these cells undergo apoptosis in the blood and liver.
HCV-specific CD4+ and CD8+ T cell responses are impaired in the acute and chronic phases of HCV infection.

the majority of CD8+ T-cells in the peripheral blood of HCV patients undergoing the acute phase are in the “death phase,” and that the majority of HCV specific CD8+ Tcells in the peripheral blood during the chronic phase of infection are in a “resting phase.”
The main takeaway from our work is that

HCV-specific CD4+ and CD8+ T cell responses are highly dysregulated in chronic infection and are associated with high levels of apoptosis, low levels of effector functions and a failure to clear the virus.
the HCV-specific T cells in the liver are undergoing apoptosis.
the HCV-specific T cells in the acute and chronic phases of infection are highly activated, expressing an effector phenotype.
